solution.concept_anchor: Prinsep 1837 — Brahmi decipherment using bilingual coins
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1857) is deceptive because 1857 is among the most memorable years in Indian history (First War of Independence), causing students to pattern-match to a familiar year rather than the correct 1837.
elimination_logic: The decipherment of Brahmi is one of the most precisely dated events in Indian historical scholarship — 1837 is the standard year.
Eliminate 1827: Too early — Prinsep's definitive Brahmi work had not yet occurred.
Eliminate 1857: Famous year for another reason entirely; no connection to Prinsep's decipherment.
Eliminate 1847: Prinsep died in 1840 — a decipherment in 1847 would be posthumous and is incorrect.
1837 is the correct year — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the proximity of 1837 to the historically dominant year 1857. Under exam pressure, students who half-remember '18-something' as the decipherment year will anchor to the most salient year in that decade — 1857 — rather than the correct 1837. Additionally, 1847 is close enough to feel plausible. Only students who have specifically memorised 1837 will resist the pull of these nearby distractors.
solution.final_explanation:
James Prinsep's decipherment of Brahmi in 1837 is the foundational event of Indian epigraphy — without it, the entire corpus of Ashokan inscriptions would remain unread.

• Option (a) — 1837: Correct. Prinsep, then Secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, used bilingual Greek-Brahmi coin legends as his key — similar methodology to Champollion's use of the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian hieroglyphics.
• Option (b) — 1827: Incorrect. Prinsep's definitive Brahmi decipherment had not occurred this early; he was engaged in other numismatic and epigraphic work during this period.
• Option (c) — 1857: Incorrect. 1857 marks the First War of Independence — Prinsep had died in 1840, making a 1857 decipherment by him impossible.
• Option (d) — 1847: Incorrect. Prinsep died in 1840 after a mental breakdown — his great work was complete by 1837–1838.

Value Addition:
• Prinsep died in 1840, just three years after his greatest achievement — he did not live to see the full scholarly impact of his decipherment.
• William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 — Prinsep built on this institutional tradition.
• Brahmi decipherment enabled the identification of Chandragupta Maurya's synchronism with Seleucus Nicator, anchoring Indian chronology to Greek records.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because it correctly matches the Kandahar Greek Edict with Greek content but swaps the script description of the Kandahar Bilingual Edict, attributing Kharosthi to it rather than Aramaic.
elimination_logic: Kandahar Greek Edict: Greek language and script only — no Aramaic, no Kharosthi. Match A with 2.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap operates on the Kandahar Bilingual Edict's script composition. Students who know Kharosthi is the 'other' non-Brahmi Ashokan script and that Kandahar is a non-Brahmi site may assume Kharosthi appears there. The precise fact is that Kandahar uses Greek and Aramaic only — Kharosthi never appears at Kandahar. Taxila and Laghman use Aramaic alone; Kandahar uses Greek alone or Greek+Aramaic together.
solution.final_explanation:
The western and northwestern Ashokan inscriptions use non-Indic scripts, but the specific combinations at each site are precise and tested.

Correct matches:
• A (Kandahar Greek Edict) → 2 (Written exclusively in Greek language and script): This is the Greek-only inscription at Kandahar, communicating Dhamma to Hellenistic settlers.
• B (Kandahar Bilingual Edict) → 4 (Written in both Greek and Aramaic — the only Ashokan inscription with two non-Indic scripts): This bilingual edict is unique in the entire corpus.
• C (Taxila Aramaic Edict) → 1 (Standalone Aramaic inscription reflecting the pre-Mauryan Achaemenid scribal tradition): Taxila's Achaemenid heritage made Aramaic the natural scribal choice.
• D (Laghman Aramaic Edict) → 3 (Aramaic inscription in modern Afghanistan, reflecting continuity with the Achaemenid administrative zone): Laghman (ancient Lampaka) was in the Achaemenid cultural sphere.

Trap pairing to watch: B (Bilingual Edict) → 4 requires knowing the second script is Aramaic, not Kharosthi.

Value Addition:
• Laghman (ancient Lampaka or Nagara) is in Nangarhar Province, modern Afghanistan — very close to the Kabul River.
• The Kandahar site (Shar-i-Kuna) has yielded both inscriptions — excavated in the 1960s by French archaeologists.
• Aramaic at Taxila and Laghman represents the easternmost extent of the Achaemenid scribal zone — these regions were Persian satrapies before Chandragupta's conquest.

solution.concept_anchor: Kharosthi right-to-left directionality — Aramaic inheritance
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Kharosthi is written right-to-left, and it is the only Ashokan script with this directional feature. Brahmi, Greek, and Aramaic in Ashokan context run left-to-right. Yes, A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Aramaic is indeed a Semitic abjad written right-to-left, and Kharosthi derives from it. Yes, R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — Aramaic's right-to-left directionality is directly inherited by Kharosthi as its derived script. R does causally explain A — Kharosthi writes right-to-left because its Aramaic parent wrote right-to-left.

Both A and R correct + R explains A — this should be option (a). Wait — re-examine: A states Kharosthi is the only Ashokan script written right-to-left. Aramaic is also written right-to-left. Does this make A false? No — A says 'only Ashokan script written right-to-left', meaning among Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek — the only one is Kharosthi. Aramaic is also right-to-left but A is about Ashokan scripts. A is correct. R explains A causally. Option (a).

Recheck: Both A and R correct and R explains A = option (a). But wait — the question must avoid option (a) as the too-obvious answer per the 30% rule. However, the causal relationship is genuine here. Correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Kharosthi's right-to-left direction is a direct inheritance from its Aramaic parent — a concrete example of script evolution preserving directional convention from ancestral writing systems.

• Assertion (A) — Correct: Among all scripts used in Ashokan inscriptions, Kharosthi alone runs right-to-left. Brahmi, Greek, and Aramaic-as-used-at-Kandahar all run left-to-right. Note: Aramaic itself is also right-to-left, but A is specifically comparing Ashokan scripts' directionality, where Kharosthi's uniqueness lies.
• Reason (R) — Correct: Aramaic, a Semitic abjad, is written right-to-left — a convention shared by Hebrew, Phoenician, and related scripts. Kharosthi, derived from Aramaic, preserved this directional feature.
• Causal link — Valid: R causally explains A. Kharosthi's right-to-left writing direction is not arbitrary — it was directly inherited from Aramaic's right-to-left convention. This is a genuine causal relationship between script lineage and directional feature.

Value Addition:
• Among the world's major script families, Semitic scripts (Arabic, Hebrew, Aramaic) typically run right-to-left; Indo-European scripts derived from Phoenician (Greek, Latin) reversed to left-to-right.
• Boustrophedon (alternating directions line-by-line) appears in some very early Greek inscriptions — a transitional phase between right-to-left Phoenician and fixed left-to-right Greek.
• All Brahmi-derived scripts (Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, etc.) write left-to-right — consistent with Brahmi's own indigenous or non-Semitic directional convention.

solution.concept_anchor: Minor rock edicts naming 'Ashoka' — Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, Udegolam

statement_analysis.statement: Ashoka used the epithets 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' (Beloved of the Gods, of Gracious Mien) as his royal self-reference in the majority of his inscriptions.
statement_analysis.reason: Across the Major Rock Edicts, Major Pillar Edicts, and most other inscriptions, Ashoka identifies himself only through these epithets — not by his personal name.

statement_analysis.statement: The personal name 'Ashoka' appears in only four minor rock edicts: Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, and Udegolam.
statement_analysis.reason: These four minor rock edicts are the only inscriptions in which the name 'Ashoka' is explicitly used alongside the standard epithets, making them uniquely significant for historical identification.

statement_analysis.statement: The connection between 'Piyadassi' and the historical king Ashoka was established during James Prinsep's own lifetime, immediately after the 1837 decipherment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Piyadassi–Ashoka equation was not immediately obvious after decipherment — the epigraphic confirmation came only in 1915 with the discovery of the Maski inscription. Prinsep died in 1840 before this connection was definitively established through epigraphy.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 only incorrect) tempts students who have read that epithets like 'Beloved of the Gods' were used by other rulers too and may doubt Statement 1's specificity — without realising Statement 3 is the false one.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' as the standard self-reference in most inscriptions — this is a well-established textbook fact. Mark Correct (not the incorrect one).
Statement 2: Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, Udegolam as the four explicit-name inscriptions — confirmed by epigraphic scholarship. Mark Correct.

Statement 3: The Piyadassi–Ashoka connection established 'immediately after 1837 during Prinsep's lifetime' — Prinsep died in 1840; the epigraphic confirmation via Maski came in 1915. This is NOT correct.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 3 extends the significance of Prinsep's 1837 decipherment too far, claiming it immediately resolved the Piyadassi–Ashoka identification. A student who knows decipherment led to historical knowledge will assume the identification followed quickly. In reality, the Pali chronicles (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa) were used to suggest the Piyadassi–Ashoka connection, but the epigraphic confirmation (Maski inscription, 1915) came 78 years after Prinsep's death. The 'immediately + during his lifetime' double qualification makes Statement 3 false.
solution.final_explanation:
The identification of Piyadassi with Ashoka is a historiographical milestone that unfolded over decades, not immediately upon decipherment.

• Statement 1 — Correct: 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' is Ashoka's consistent royal self-identification across all Major Rock Edicts, Major Pillar Edicts, and most special inscriptions. These are epithets, not a personal name.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Only four minor rock edicts — Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, and Udegolam — use the name 'Ashoka' explicitly. All four are in the Deccan/Karnataka-MP region, written in Brahmi.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: Prinsep's decipherment in 1837 made the inscriptions readable, but the explicit epigraphic confirmation that Piyadassi = Ashoka came only in 1915 (Maski discovery). Prinsep died in 1840 — three years after his breakthrough. The Piyadassi–Ashoka equation was first suggested through cross-referencing Pali chronicles, not confirmed epigraphically until 1915.

Value Addition:
• 'Devanampiya' was also used as an epithet by Sri Lankan kings — showing the term's broader ancient South Asian royal vocabulary.
• The Mahavamsa (Sri Lankan chronicle, c. 5th century CE) is a key text that associates 'Piyadassi' with an Ashokan-type figure.
• Udegolam (Karnataka) and Nittur (Karnataka) are less commonly taught minor rock edict sites — worth memorising alongside Maski and Gujarra.

solution.concept_anchor: Ashoka's script choice — inclusion strategy vs. Achaemenid comparison

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: Ashoka's use of multiple scripts and languages in his inscriptions represents a 'bottom-up communication' strategy aimed at maximising accessibility of Dhamma among diverse populations, rather than imposing a single imperial script.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately characterises Ashoka's approach — using local scripts (Greek for Hellenistic settlers, Kharosthi for the northwestern frontier, Brahmi for the heartland) to reach ordinary people in their familiar writing systems, prioritising reception over centralisation.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: This multilingual approach was entirely unprecedented in the ancient world — no earlier imperial tradition had employed multiple scripts in royal inscriptions before Ashoka.
statement_analysis.reason: The Achaemenid Behistun inscription of Darius I (c. 522 BCE) used three scripts (Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian cuneiform) — a clear multilingual imperial precedent approximately 250 years before Ashoka.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) tempts students who admire Ashoka's multilingual model and have not specifically recalled the Achaemenid Behistun precedent, leading them to accept the 'unprecedented' claim in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: The characterisation of Ashoka's script strategy as bottom-up, accessibility-first communication is academically established and accurate. Statement 1 is Correct.

Test Statement 2: The Achaemenid Behistun inscription predates Ashoka by approximately 250 years and uses three scripts/languages — it is a direct precedent for multilingual imperial epigraphy. The claim of 'entirely unprecedented' is false. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2 is the word 'entirely unprecedented'. Ashoka's scale and the specific combination of scripts are distinctive, but the broader practice of multilingual royal inscriptions was established by the Achaemenids. A student who focuses on Ashoka's unique contextual significance may not recall that the Behistun inscription (a staple of world history) predates him with exactly the same multilingual principle. The trap works by replacing 'innovative in the Indian context' (true) with 'unprecedented in the ancient world' (false).
solution.final_explanation:
Ashoka's multilingual inscription strategy is remarkable and historically significant — but it was not without precedent in the broader ancient world.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ashoka's script choices follow a consistent logic: use the script familiar to the local population. This is a deliberate communication policy — Greek for Kandahar, Kharosthi for Shahbazgarhi, Brahmi for the subcontinent. It prioritises reception over the imperial convenience of uniformity.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Achaemenid Empire's Behistun inscription (c. 522 BCE, Darius I) uses Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian cuneiform in parallel — a tri-script royal proclamation approximately 250 years before Ashoka. Multilingual royal epigraphy was an Achaemenid practice Ashoka may have encountered through his northwest frontier's administrative traditions.

Value Addition:
• The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt) is another multilingual royal inscription — Egyptian hieroglyphics, Demotic, and Greek — showing this was a pan-ancient-world practice.
• Ashoka's specific innovation was using scripts of the subject population for moral/religious content, not just administrative announcements — a qualitative difference in purpose.
• The Achaemenid administrative presence in Taxila and Gandhara directly transmitted the multilingual epigraphy model to the Mauryan court through scribal traditions.

This requires knowing the classification system, not just the existence of the edicts.
solution.final_explanation:
The numerical classification of Ashokan inscriptions requires precision — not just knowing categories exist but knowing their exact counts and classification boundaries.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Major Rock Edict series comprises 14 edicts in the standard series — this is the foundational epigraphic count.
• Statement 2 — Correct: There are 7 Major Pillar Edicts — Pillar Edicts I through VII form the canonical series on the Ashokan stone columns.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Separate Kalinga Edicts (at Dhauli and Jaugada, Odisha) replace Rock Edicts XII and XIII at those specific sites but are classified as a separate category from the standard 14 Major Rock Edicts. They are not a subset of the 14 — they are the regional variant content at Kalinga sites.
• Statement 4 — Correct: All seven Major Pillar Edicts are in Brahmi — the geographic placement of pillars in the Gangetic heartland and Buddhist pilgrimage routes explains this Brahmi exclusivity.

Value Addition:
• Pillar Edict VII is the longest of the seven — it provides a retrospective summary of Ashoka's Dhamma activities.
• The Barabar Cave inscriptions are a fourth category (besides Major/Minor Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts) — short, different in purpose (Ajivika donations), not Dhamma proclamations.
• Dhauli and Jaugada (both Odisha) are the sites where Kalinga-specific substitute edicts appear — reflecting Ashoka's special sensitivity toward his most traumatic conquest.

solution.concept_anchor: Northwestern India script succession — Aramaic to Kharosthi to Brahmi-era displacement
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c places Kharosthi before Achaemenid Aramaic, which sounds plausible to students who think of Kharosthi as an ancient indigenous script rather than a derivative of the later-arriving Aramaic administrative tradition.
elimination_logic: Achaemenid rule in northwestern India (c. 6th–4th century BCE) brought Aramaic as the administrative language — this precedes Mauryan rule.
Kharosthi emerged as a derivative of Aramaic during or shortly after the Achaemenid period — it could not have preceded Aramaic's establishment in the region.
Ashokan use of both Aramaic and Kharosthi reflects the mid-3rd century BCE moment — Aramaic as legacy, Kharosthi as its Indic adaptation.
Post-Mauryan Gupta-era Brahmi-derived scripts gradually displaced Kharosthi in the northwest by the 4th century CE — the final stage.
Correct sequence: Achaemenid Aramaic → Kharosthi emergence → Ashokan dual use → Kharosthi extinction/Brahmi-based scripts prevail. Option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap inverts the Aramaic-Kharosthi relationship. A student who sees Kharosthi as 'older' and 'more indigenous' than Aramaic may place it before Achaemenid Aramaic in the sequence. The critical fact is that Kharosthi is a derivative of Aramaic — it cannot predate the establishment of Aramaic scribal practices in the northwest. The Achaemenid conquest of Gandhara and Sindh (c. 519 BCE) brought Aramaic; Kharosthi emerged from that tradition, predating Ashoka's edicts but postdating Achaemenid Aramaic.
solution.final_explanation:
The script history of northwestern India represents successive layers of imperial cultural influence — Achaemenid, Mauryan, and post-Mauryan — each leaving a scribal trace.

Correct chronological sequence:
(i) Achaemenid Aramaic established in northwestern India (c. 6th–4th century BCE) → (ii) Kharosthi emerges as an Indic adaptation of Aramaic (c. 4th–3rd century BCE) → (iii) Ashoka uses both Aramaic and Kharosthi at northwestern sites while Brahmi dominates the heartland (mid-3rd century BCE) → (iv) Kharosthi becomes extinct (c. 4th century CE) as Brahmi-derived Gupta-era scripts spread into the northwest.

• Option (a) — Correct: This sequence correctly places Achaemenid Aramaic first, Kharosthi as its derivative, and eventual Brahmi-era displacement last.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Placing Kharosthi before Aramaic is the classic derivation-reversal error.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Starting with indigenous Indic scripts before Aramaic ignores the Achaemenid foundation of Kharosthi.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Placing Brahmi displacement before Ashokan usage is chronologically inverted.

Value Addition:
• Cyrus the Great and Darius I brought Aramaic to the Indus region — Taxila (Takshashila) was a major Achaemenid satrapal centre.
• The Niya documents (from Silk Road Niya site) show Kharosthi in use as late as the 3rd–4th century CE — the script's final phase.
• After Kharosthi's extinction, the Sharada script (Kashmir) and later Gupta-Brahmi derivatives filled the scribal role in the northwest.

solution.concept_anchor: Indo-Greek bilingual coins as key for Kharosthi decipherment
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students know Prinsep used bilingual coins for Brahmi decipherment and may assume the same Greek-Brahmi coins served for Kharosthi — without recalling that the Kharosthi coins have Kharosthi (not Brahmi) on the reverse, and the coins are Indo-Greek (not just Greek-Brahmi).
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Greek-Brahmi bilingual coins were used for Brahmi decipherment — not for Kharosthi. Conflating the two decipherments' coin types is the trap.

Eliminate option (c): Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts appear in both Brahmi and Kharosthi at different sites — they do not present both scripts on the same inscription, making them unsuitable as bilingual keys for Kharosthi.
Eliminate option (d): Aramaic-Brahmi parallel texts do not exist as an established decipherment tool — this is a plausible-fabrication distractor.
Option (b) is correct: Indo-Greek bilingual coins with Greek on the obverse and Kharosthi on the reverse were the specific key Prinsep used to crack Kharosthi.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap substitutes 'Greek-Brahmi bilingual coins' (used for Brahmi decipherment) for 'Indo-Greek coins with Kharosthi reverse' (used for Kharosthi decipherment). A student who remembers 'Prinsep used bilingual coins' without distinguishing which coins for which script will select option (a). The distinction requires knowing that two different sets of bilingual coins were used: Greek-Brahmi for Brahmi, and Greek-Kharosthi (Indo-Greek coins) for Kharosthi.
solution.final_explanation:
Prinsep's methodology for cracking both Brahmi and Kharosthi relied on bilingual evidence — but the specific coins used were different for each script.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Greek-Brahmi bilingual coins were used to decipher Brahmi, not Kharosthi. These coins circulated in regions where Greek and Brahmi scripts overlapped — different from the Indo-Greek coin zone where Kharosthi appeared.
• Option (b) — Correct: Indo-Greek bilingual coins — carrying Greek legends on the obverse (the Greek royal portrait side) and Kharosthi legends on the reverse — provided Prinsep with the parallel text needed to systematically decode Kharosthi's letter values.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ashokan Rock Edicts do not present Brahmi and Kharosthi bilingually at the same site — they use one or the other. A bilingual inscription key requires the same text in two scripts at one location.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: No established Aramaic-Brahmi parallel text evidence was used for Kharosthi decipherment — this is a fabricated option.

Value Addition:
• The Indo-Greek kings (successors of Alexander's Bactrian successors) ruled northwestern India c. 180–10 BCE — their bilingual coins thus postdate Ashoka but were available to 19th-century scholars for analysis.
• Menander I (Milinda) is the most famous Indo-Greek king — his coins with Kharosthi legends were among those Prinsep analysed.
• Christian Lassen subsequently identified the Kharosthi vowel markers using Prinsep's consonantal framework — a supplementary contribution to the full decipherment.

solution.concept_anchor: Brahmi origin debate — indigenous vs. Semitic derivation

statement_analysis.statement: One school of scholarly thought holds that Brahmi script developed indigenously in India, possibly from the Indus Valley script tradition, without Semitic derivation.
statement_analysis.reason: The indigenous origin theory is a legitimate and respected scholarly position — proponents argue that Brahmi's structure does not map neatly onto Aramaic or Phoenician and that it shows signs of systematic independent creation.

statement_analysis.statement: Another school argues that Brahmi is derived from a Semitic script (Aramaic or Phoenician), adapted to represent Indic phonemes — a view supported by certain structural and historical parallels.
statement_analysis.reason: The Semitic derivation hypothesis notes structural parallels between Brahmi consonant shapes and Aramaic letters and points to the same direction of writing influence — this is the other major scholarly position in the Brahmi origin debate.

statement_analysis.statement: The debate over Brahmi's origin has been definitively resolved in favour of the indigenous development theory by modern computational linguistics.
statement_analysis.reason: No consensus has been reached — the origin of Brahmi remains one of the open questions in ancient Indian scholarship; neither theory has been definitively proven using computational linguistics or any other method.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who have read about 'modern computational' studies on script evolution and assume such methods have settled the debate.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Indigenous origin as a legitimate scholarly theory — accurate representation of the debate. Mark Correct.
Statement 2: Semitic derivation as the competing theory with structural evidence — also accurate. Mark Correct.
Statement 3: 'Definitively resolved' by computational linguistics — this is false; the debate remains open in the scholarly literature. Mark Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct; Statement 3 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 3 uses the phrase 'definitively resolved' — a claim that sounds authoritative and modern. Students who have vaguely read about computational approaches to ancient scripts may accept this. The Brahmi origin debate is, in fact, one of the most persistently contested questions in Indian historical linguistics — no consensus exists. Any claim of 'definitive resolution' should trigger skepticism.
solution.final_explanation:
The origin of Brahmi is one of ancient India's most debated epigraphic questions — engaging historians, linguists, and archaeologists without reaching consensus.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The indigenous development theory holds that Brahmi was systematically devised by Indian scholars, possibly for recording Prakrit, without dependence on external models. Proponents cite the mismatch between Brahmi letter forms and Aramaic equivalents.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Semitic derivation theory notes that Brahmi appears rather suddenly in a mature, complete form — suggesting adaptation from an existing system (Aramaic/Phoenician) rather than gradual indigenous development. Both theories have credible scholarly support.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Computational linguistic analyses have been applied to this question but have not produced a consensus resolution. The debate remains active. Declaring 'definitive resolution' misrepresents the current state of scholarship.

Value Addition:
• The Indus Valley script (still undeciphered) is sometimes cited in indigenous origin arguments — but the ~1,500-year gap between Indus script disappearance and Brahmi's appearance makes direct lineage hard to prove.
• Brahmi's completeness and systematic phonemic coverage at its earliest known appearance (Ashokan inscriptions) is a central puzzle in the origin debate.
• Tamil-Brahmi's early appearance alongside Ashokan Brahmi shows the script was adapted regionally almost immediately — evidence of its flexibility and systematic design.

solution.concept_anchor: Eusebeia — Greek term for Dhamma in Kandahar edict
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b ('philanthropia') is deceptive because it is a genuine Greek philosophical term meaning 'love of humanity' — plausible for Dhamma's ethical content — but it is not the specific term used in the Kandahar edict.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): 'Arête' means virtue/excellence in Greek — a legitimate philosophical concept but not the documented Kandahar edict term.
Eliminate option (b): 'Philanthropia' (love of humanity) is plausible for Dhamma's compassion dimension but is not the attested term in the Kandahar inscription.
Eliminate option (d): 'Sophia' means wisdom — again a genuine Greek term but not the specific word used in the Kandahar edict for Dhamma.
Option (c): 'Eusebeia' meaning piety/reverence is the documented term used in the Kandahar Greek edict as the Greek equivalent of Dhamma — option (c) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap operates by presenting three genuine Greek philosophical terms (arête, philanthropia, sophia) alongside the correct answer (eusebeia). A student who knows Kandahar's Greek edict uses a Greek philosophical equivalent for Dhamma but has not memorised the specific term will be drawn to 'philanthropia' (compassion/love of humanity) as the most intuitive semantic match for Dhamma's ethical dimension. 'Eusebeia' (piety/reverence toward gods and social norms) is the actual documented term — less obvious but historically attested.
solution.final_explanation:
The Kandahar Greek Edict's translation of Dhamma into Greek vocabulary reveals Ashoka's engagement with Hellenistic philosophical discourse — the specific term chosen is 'eusebeia'.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 'Arête' means excellence or moral virtue in the Aristotelian tradition — a defensible choice but not the attested Kandahar term.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'Philanthropia' (love of humanity) is semantically close to Dhamma's compassion dimension but is not the term used in the inscription.
• Option (c) — Correct: 'Eusebeia' means piety, reverence, or proper conduct toward gods and fellow humans — the Greek term that most closely maps onto Dhamma's connotations of right conduct, respect, and moral order. This is the documented word in the Kandahar Greek Edict.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 'Sophia' means wisdom or knowledge — relevant to the philosophical register but not the specific term chosen for Dhamma.

Value Addition:
• 'Eusebeia' is also central to Stoic philosophy — suggesting the Kandahar edict may have been drafted with Stoic-influenced Greek intellectuals in mind.
• The use of a Greek philosophical term for Dhamma — rather than a phonetic transliteration — confirms the intent was genuine cross-cultural communication.
• Parallel translations of Dhamma in Aramaic inscriptions also use equivalent ethical terms from that tradition — showing systematic cross-cultural philosophical translation.
